Autumn Riding by Region

Autumn is many experienced tourers' favourite season. The crowds vanish, the light turns golden, and the landscape blazes with colour. But conditions deteriorate as the season progresses, and choosing the right region at the right time maximises your enjoyment.

September: The Golden Month (Anywhere)

  • Scottish Highlands (★★★★★): September is arguably the best touring month. No midges, warm days, birch woods turning gold, and empty roads as tourists leave.
  • Lake District (★★★★★): Post-summer calm. The fells start changing colour and the lakes are mirror-calm.
  • Snowdonia (★★★★★): Quiet roads, warm enough for passes, autumn beginning in the oak woods.
  • All regions (★★★★+): September is universally good. Ride your favourite.

October: Colour Peak

  • Perthshire (★★★★★): Scotland's autumn colour capital. The Big Tree Country around Pitlochry is extraordinary.
  • Wye Valley (★★★★★): The gorge woodland blazes with colour. The A466 is at its most beautiful.
  • New Forest (★★★★★): Ancient beeches and oaks turn spectacular colours. The forest roads are magical.
  • North York Moors (★★★★): Heather fading but the woodland colours are building. Atmospheric moorland.
  • Scottish Highlands (★★★): Getting cold, days shortening, but the colour is still beautiful on clear days.

November: Narrowing Options

  • South Coast (★★★★): Mild enough for riding. Devon, Dorset, Hampshire offer sheltered routes.
  • Cotswolds (★★★): Late autumn colour in a sheltered landscape. Short rides between villages.
  • Wales/Scotland (★★): Cold, wet, short days. Only for the committed.
Autumn follows the reverse pattern to spring — colour progresses from north to south and from mountains to lowlands. Start in Scotland in September, move to central England in October, and finish in the south in November.

Autumn Riding Gear

Autumn is the season of layers. Mornings can be near-freezing while afternoons reach 15°C. A layering system — thermal base layer, fleece mid-layer, and waterproof outer — allows you to adjust throughout the day. Remove layers at lunchtime, add them back as the afternoon cools.

Visibility is a growing concern in autumn. Shorter days, low sun, and murky conditions make high-visibility gear more important than in summer. A hi-vis vest over your riding jacket costs little and makes you significantly more visible to other road users in the gloom of an October afternoon.

Autumn tyres need attention. Cooler road temperatures mean less grip, and wet fallen leaves create treacherous surfaces. Check tyre pressures more frequently as temperatures drop — air pressure decreases with temperature, and under-inflated tyres reduce both grip and handling precision. keyTakeaways: Autumn colour progresses north to south, the reverse of spring: Scotland in September, central England in October, the south in November.
September is universally excellent, with no midges, warm days, golden birch woods, and roads emptying of tourists.
October is peak colour, with Perthshire, the Wye Valley, and the New Forest at their most spectacular.
November narrows the options to the milder south coast and sheltered Cotswolds.
Wet fallen leaves and cooler road temperatures reduce grip, so check pressures more often and layer up for cold mornings.

faq.q: Why do many tourers prefer autumn?
faq.a: The crowds vanish, the light turns golden, and the landscape blazes with colour. September in particular offers warm days, no midges, and empty roads as summer tourists leave. For experienced riders who value quiet roads and atmosphere over guaranteed warmth, autumn is often the favourite season.

faq.q: Where is best for autumn colour?
faq.a: October is peak colour. Perthshire around Pitlochry, known as Big Tree Country, is Scotland's autumn capital. The Wye Valley gorge woodland along the A466 is stunning, and the ancient beeches and oaks of the New Forest turn spectacular. Follow the colour south as the month progresses.

faq.q: What gear matters most in autumn?
faq.a: Layers. Mornings can be near-freezing while afternoons reach 15C, so a thermal base layer, fleece mid-layer, and waterproof outer let you adjust through the day. High-visibility gear matters more than in summer because of shorter days, low sun, and murky conditions that make you harder to see.

faq.q: What are the main autumn road hazards?
faq.a: Wet fallen leaves create treacherous surfaces, especially in corners and on tree-lined lanes, and cooler road temperatures mean less grip overall. Check tyre pressures more frequently, since air pressure drops with temperature and under-inflated tyres reduce grip and handling. Low autumn sun can also dazzle, so a clear visor and sunglasses help.
